passage: In the Kraków flat, Sunday lunch was over. Paula's mother stacked the plates. "Paula, come and dry these, please." Paula looked at the sofa. Her brother Marek, twelve, was already stretched out with his tablet, one sock hanging off the armrest. Nobody called him. Paula took the towel. The water ran warm, and forks clattered in the sink. She counted the plates as she dried them: fourteen. Through the doorway she could hear the cheering of a game. She did not say anything. She dried the last cup very slowly and set it on the shelf, then looked at the towel in her hand, wet all the way through.

qa.q: How many plates did Paula count?
qa.a: Paula counted fourteen plates.

qa.q: What might Paula be feeling as she dries the last cup very slowly?
qa.a: She is probably resentful and tired. She notices that nobody called Marek, yet she says nothing.

qa.q: What choice did Paula make about speaking up, and what else could be tried?
qa.a: Paula stayed silent and dried slowly. She could calmly ask whether Marek can dry the next round, or her mother could call both children.

qa.q: How might Marek see the afternoon?
qa.a: He may not notice anything unfair, since nobody called him and he is absorbed in his game.

grounding: A girl is asked to help in the kitchen while her brother plays, and she notices the difference without saying a word.

passage: At the Diwali fair at the community centre, Uma, nine, was sent to the kitchen counter to help make puris. Her brother Ravi, eleven, was allowed to go and play carrom with the boys in the hall. Uma rolled out puris beside two other girls while the carrom coins clacked in the next room. She said nothing but looked at the doorway twice. Charu, the volunteer in charge of the kitchen rota, noticed. She wiped her hands. "Helpers, everyone washes hands and comes to the counter, boys and girls. Ravi, come, you're on laddus." Ravi groaned, then shaped one lopsided laddu and glanced at Uma as if to check. Uma pressed a puri flat and half smiled.

qa.q: What was Ravi allowed to do in the hall?
qa.a: Ravi was allowed to play carrom with the boys in the hall.

qa.q: What is Uma likely feeling as she looks at the doorway twice?
qa.a: Uma probably feels left out and a little resentful, though she says nothing.

qa.q: What turning point came when Charu spoke?
qa.a: Charu called all helpers, boys and girls, to the counter and put Ravi on laddus, so the work was shared and Uma no longer worked alone.

qa.q: Why might Charu have stepped in?
qa.a: Charu noticed Uma's glances at the doorway and saw that the work was unevenly split, so she changed the rota.

grounding: A girl is sent to work in the kitchen while her brother plays, and notices the unfairness without words until an adult shares the tasks.

passage:
Last Christmas, when I was nine, we went to Aunty's house for lunch. Aunty said, "Elizabeth, come help. Girls help in the kitchen."
I peeled potatoes for a long time. My fingers smelled of onions. Through the door I could see my cousin Siddharth playing carrom with the uncles. He was eleven. Nobody called him.
I didn't say anything. But I kept looking at the carrom board, and I peeled slower and slower.
Later my Mummy found me by the sink. She looked at me, then at the carrom board. She didn't say much. She just walked out and said, "Siddharth, come, you can wash the plates with Elizabeth."
He grumbled. We washed together, and he splashed me, and I splashed back.

qa.q: What was Siddharth playing?
qa.a: Siddharth was playing carrom with the uncles.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth peeling slower and slower suggest she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt left out and that it was unfair, even though she didn't say anything.

qa.q: How did Mummy handle it well?
qa.a: She noticed without Elizabeth saying a word and quietly called Siddharth to share the washing, showing both children that chores are shared.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see the chores after that day?
qa.a: He grumbled at first, but washing plates with Elizabeth may teach him that helping in the kitchen is for boys too.

grounding: A girl is sent to the kitchen while a boy cousin plays, notices the unfairness without words, and an adult quietly shares the chore.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 4B, Thursday.
In art today I asked the children to draw "My Sunday." Disha drew herself at the sink, a pile of plates, and a boy outside with a kite. When I asked who the boy was, she said, "My brother. He gets to fly kites. I help Mummy." She said it plainly, without complaint, but she coloured the kite very carefully, three times over.
I did not comment in class. After school I rang her mother, Tanuja, and told her about the drawing, only what I had seen. Tanuja was quiet, then said, "I never noticed. I did the same at her age." She said she would ask Disha's brother to share the dishes this weekend and let Disha fly the kite too.

qa.q: What did Disha draw herself doing?
qa.a: Disha drew herself at the sink with a pile of plates.

qa.q: What might Disha colouring the kite three times over suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she wished she could fly the kite too, and may have felt left out, though she said it without complaint.

qa.q: What small step did the teacher take, and why was it wise?
qa.a: The teacher told Tanuja privately and only described the drawing, which let Tanuja notice the pattern herself without shaming Disha or the family.

qa.q: How might Tanuja be affected by hearing about the drawing?
qa.a: Tanuja seems surprised and thoughtful, recognising that she did the same as a child, and decides to share chores more fairly.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a girl doing dishes while her brother plays, noticing it without words, and her mother deciding to share chores fairly.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today after school Amma called me to roll chapatis. Mohit was watching cartoons. I asked, "Why not Mohit?" Amma said, "He's a boy, Gopika. Boys don't roll."
I rolled eleven chapatis. Some were not round. Mohit came and ate three and said mine looked like maps.
I was angry but I didn't know why exactly. It's just chapatis.
At night Appa came home and saw me rubbing my arm. He asked why. I told him. Appa said, "Mohit, tomorrow you roll, and Gopika watches cartoons." Mohit made a face.
Then Appa said he would roll too! His chapati looked like a map of Africa. We laughed so much.
I think tomorrow will be fair.
Gopika

qa.q: How many chapatis did Gopika roll?
qa.a: Gopika rolled eleven chapatis.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling after rolling the chapatis?
qa.a: Gopika felt angry, though she didn't know exactly why, because Mohit watched cartoons while she worked.

qa.q: How did Appa make things fairer?
qa.a: Appa asked Mohit to roll the next day and rolled chapatis himself, showing that cooking is for everyone.

qa.q: What would change if Appa hadn't noticed Gopika rubbing her arm?
qa.a: Gopika might keep rolling every day while Mohit played, and both children would learn that chores depend on being a girl or a boy.

grounding: A girl rolls chapatis while her brother plays, feels the unfairness before she can name it, and a parent shares the chore fairly.

passage: In the courtyard of their house near Sitapur, Sarika chachi called, "Sarita, come, roll the rotis." Sarita, ten, put down her book and went. Outside, her brother Mohan and the cousins were playing gilli-danda, shouting. Nobody called Mohan. Sarita rolled roti after roti, flour up to her elbows, and watched through the door. When the rotis were done, Mohan ran in first and was served first. Sarita said nothing. She just looked at her floury hands, then at his muddy ones. That night she asked Dadi, "Why does Mohan never roll?" Dadi paused, as if she had never been asked. "Hmm," she said. "Maybe tomorrow he will."

qa.q: What was Mohan playing?
qa.a: Gilli-danda, with the cousins.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling as she watched Mohan through the door?
qa.a: She felt quietly hurt and aware something was unfair, though she said nothing.

qa.q: What could Sarika chachi do to make chores fair?
qa.a: She could call both Sarita and Mohan to help, and serve everyone together, so both children learn that work is shared.

qa.q: How might Dadi have seen Sarita's question?
qa.a: Dadi seemed surprised and thoughtful, as if she had never questioned who does the rolling before.

grounding: It illustrates a girl asked to help in the kitchen while her brother plays, who notices the unfairness before she can name it.
